newsitem.title: ANGOLA: IMF due in Angola next week to review economy.
newsitem.headline: IMF due in Angola next week to review economy.

text.p: LUANDA, May 22 ( Reuter) - The International Monetary Fund is due in Angola next week to assess the country's economic reforms before implementing a three-year emergency programme agreed upon last year, economists say.
The World Bank representative in Luanda, Philip Owusu, said the bank was also ready to clear over $250 million in loans to rebuild war-ravaged Angola if the IMF visit was successful.

"The Bank has between $250 million and $300 million ready for Angola. If the IMF visit goes well it will not only pave the way for these loans to go forward, but will send a favourable signal to other lenders as well," he told Reuters on Wednesday.
IMF head Michel Camdessus, visiting Luanda last October, said he was convinced the government was serious about economic reform and announced a three-year emergency programme worth $75 million.

But Western economists in Luanda said the IMF did not return to Angola in January as planned to begin implementing the programme, because the government failed to hand over vital data on revenue and spending.
"I understand they have agreed to come back now because the government has finally received the numbers," an economist said.
Owusu said Angola had agreed to supply the IMF delegation with new information on the accounts of state oil companies Sonangol, the central bank, and state diamond company Endiama.
Accounts for these state institutions have been closely guarded by the government, which earns about $4 billion in oil revenue annually.
Owusu said the World Bank had nine projects in Angola since worth $270 million, mainly in infrastructure, health, education, water and transportation.
New loans would go towards resettling Angolan refugees, re-integrating demobilised soldiers, education, health and infrastructure development in mostly urban areas, he said.
Angola's official unemployment rate is about 50 percent and the per capita income is between $350 to $400 a year. External debt is about $15 billion.

Economists believe the IMF will seek further reductions in Angola's housing and fuel subsidies, a reduction in the budget deficit, increased spending on education and health, and the trimming of the civil service.
Transparency of the oil accounts will be one of the biggest issues for the IMF, economists agree.
"Together with the IMF, we will provide technical assistance to the government to do audits of the oil accounts," said Owusu.
"We will make recommendations on improving control and managerial types of changes. If the government agrees, we will provide the financing for the auditors," he said.
Oil contributes at least 40 percent to the country's gross domestic product, accounts for 90 percent of exports and 75 percent of government revenue.
Owusu said the African Development Bank, which has suspended loans to Angola because it is in arrears to the ADB, could also send a delegation soon.
"It is not inconceivable that the ADB would come back into Angola," said Owusu. "They are expected to start discussing the issue of arrears soon with the Angolans."
The World Bank would send a delegation to Angola in July to discuss high inflation, now 1,650 percent annually, he said.

Although recent figures show a decline in monthly inflation of about three percent, some economists say the figures are deceiving. They say the government owes civil servants up to six months in back wages, which will push inflation up.
Angola's fixed central bank rate for the kwanza is 196,000 to the dollar, but the black market rate is around 260,000 against the U.S. currency.
